title: The chemotherapy is late
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an oncology day unit. A problem at the pharmacy production unit means that this morning's chemotherapy hasn't arrived. Six patients have had cannulas inserted and are waiting, and some have travelled a long way.

The nurse in charge asks you to help manage the situation.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Find out from pharmacy how long the delay is likely to be.
options.brief: Accurate information is the basis for every decision.
options.detailed: Without knowing how long the delay is, you can't advise patients or plan. A quick call to pharmacy lets you give honest information.

options.text: Tell the patients that pharmacy is at fault.
options.brief: Blaming another department doesn't help and damages trust.
options.detailed: Patients need to know there is a delay, not who is to blame. Criticising colleagues in front of patients undermines confidence in the service.

options.text: Tell the patients about the delay, and when you'll update them.
options.brief: Patients cope better with delays when they are kept informed.
options.detailed: Waiting without information is stressful, especially for patients having chemotherapy. An honest explanation and a time for the next update help them plan.

options.text: Send all the patients home and rebook them.
options.brief: May be unnecessary if the delay is short.
options.detailed: Rebooking everyone without knowing the length of the delay may cause more disruption than waiting.

options.text: Ask the patients to wait without explanation until the drugs arrive.
options.brief: Leaves patients anxious and unable to plan.
options.detailed: Not telling patients about the delay is discourteous and can cause distress.

options.text: Plan with the nurse in charge for patients who can't wait.
options.brief: Some patients may need rebooking or other arrangements.
options.detailed: Some patients may have transport or other commitments. Agreeing with the nurse in charge how to handle this, such as rebooking or removing cannulas, keeps care organised.

options.text: Give the pre-medication now so they're ready when the drugs arrive.
options.brief: Pre-medication timing matters, and the delay is unknown.
options.detailed: Pre-medication is timed in relation to chemotherapy. Giving it now, without knowing when the drugs will arrive, could reduce its effect.

options.text: Phone the pharmacy manager to complain about the service.
options.brief: Complaining doesn't help the patients now.
options.detailed: The failure may need reviewing later, but a complaint now doesn't solve the problem.

explanation.issue: This tests how you manage an unexpected service failure: getting information, keeping patients informed and planning with the team.
explanation.keyDetails: The delay length is unknown. Patients are waiting with cannulas in. Some have travelled far. The nurse in charge has asked for help.
explanation.reasoning: [A] gets the facts, [C] keeps patients informed, and [F] plans for those who can't wait. The distractors blame ([B], [H]), act without information ([D], [G]), or leave patients uninformed ([E]).
explanation.competing: [D] might be right if the delay turns out to be long, but it should follow finding out, not replace it.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, keeping patients informed about their care.
